summary: Papua New Guinea occupies the eastern half of the island of New Guinea and surrounding islands, and is one of the most linguistically diverse countries in the world, with more than 800 languages.

ranking.name: Protestantism
ranking.description: Protestantism was introduced in 1871 by the London Missionary Society to the Torres Strait and the Papuan coast in the south; from the 1880s, when Germany ruled northern New Guinea, German Lutheran and Methodist missions followed. The missions divided mission territories under 'comity agreements', so that certain areas are still dominated by one denomination to this day; for example, the north is mainly Lutheran. At independence in 1975 the preamble of the constitution declared that the nation was founded on 'Christian principles', and today the main denominations include Lutheran, United Church and Pentecostal.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: The Catholic Society of the Divine Word and the Missionaries of the Sacred Heart entered the north and the island of New Britain during the German colonial period of the 1880s. After World War II the interior highlands were 'discovered' and opened up, and the Catholic and Lutheran churches competed to enter the highlands to evangelize, making Catholicism the largest single denomination, especially concentrated in East Sepik, New Britain and the Highlands.

ranking.name: Other Christian denominations
ranking.description: Other Christian denominations include Seventh-day Adventists, Baptists and Jehovah's Witnesses, as well as various evangelical and charismatic churches introduced from abroad in recent years. The Adventists arrived around 1908 and are deeply influential in some areas; for example, in some villages whole communities have adopted the faith and follow its dietary rules.

ranking.name: Traditional beliefs and others
ranking.description: Papua New Guinea has more than eight hundred ethnic groups, who traditionally believe in ancestral spirits and deities and use sorcery to explain illness and misfortune. The highlands had no contact with the outside world until the 1930s, but missionaries moved in quickly, so the population that follows purely traditional religion is now small. Many traditional ideas, such as fear of sorcery, still coexist with Christianity and even lead to violence against people accused of being witches.

religion.background: The peoples of Papua New Guinea originally believed in ancestral spirits and nature spirits, and cargo cult movements were also widespread during the colonial period. The London Missionary Society began missionary work in 1871; in the 1880s, when Germany ruled the north and Britain, and later Australia, ruled the south, the missions divided their territories. After the highlands made contact with the outside world in the 1930s, missionaries moved in quickly. At independence in 1975 the constitution declared Christian principles, and in 2025 Parliament even amended the constitution to declare the country a Christian nation, but traditional beliefs still deeply influence society.

language.official: English, Tok Pisin, Hiri Motu and Papua New Guinean Sign Language are the official languages.

ranking.name: Tok Pisin
ranking.description: Tok Pisin is an English-based creole that formed in the late 19th century as a lingua franca among Pacific Islanders recruited to work on plantations in Samoa and Queensland, and returning laborers brought it back to New Guinea. During the German and Australian periods it became the common language of plantations, missions and administration. Because Papua New Guinea has more than eight hundred languages, Tok Pisin has become the most important lingua franca in the country, and parliamentary debates are also largely conducted in it.

ranking.name: English
ranking.description: English became the language of administration and education from 1906, when Australia ruled Papua, and after World War I, when it governed New Guinea; it continued as an official language after independence in 1975, and English is used in government documents, law and education from secondary school upward. However, very few people speak English as a mother tongue, mainly elite families in the cities.

ranking.name: Hiri Motu
ranking.description: Hiri Motu derives from a simplified language used by the Motu people of the south and neighboring peoples on their traditional trading voyages (hiri). When Britain and Australia ruled Papua in the late 19th century, the police force used it as a means of communication, hence it is also called 'Police Motu'. It is mainly spoken around Port Moresby in the south, and the number of speakers is declining as Tok Pisin spreads.

language.history: Papua New Guinea has more than eight hundred languages, making it the most linguistically diverse country in the world, belonging to the Austronesian family and several dozen Papuan language families. In the late 19th century the north was ruled by Germany and the south by Britain, later taken over by Australia, and Tok Pisin and Hiri Motu became the lingua francas of the north and south respectively. After independence in 1975, English, Tok Pisin and Hiri Motu were made co-official languages, and in 2015 sign language was also made an official language, but many small languages are endangered as young people shift to Tok Pisin.

ranking.name: Mumu (earth oven)
ranking.description: A pit is dug in the ground and heated stones are placed in it; pork, chicken, sweet potato, taro and greens wrapped in banana leaves are put in, then covered with earth and slow-cooked for several hours.
ranking.history: The mumu is a traditional cooking method shared throughout Papua New Guinea. Pigs are a symbol of wealth and status in local society and are used for bride-price at weddings, compensation payments for reconciliation and important ceremonies. In highland societies, 'big men' hold large feasts at which dozens of pigs are slaughtered to demonstrate their power. The mumu remains an essential dish at village celebrations, church events and political gatherings.

ranking.name: Sago
ranking.description: The starchy pith is scraped from the trunk of the sago palm, washed with water to settle out the starch and then dried; it can be cooked into a translucent gelatinous paste or baked into cakes, with a sticky, soft texture.
ranking.history: Sago has been the staple food of the lowlands and swamp regions of New Guinea for thousands of years, and is especially important in the Sepik River basin and Gulf Province. One sago palm can supply a family with food for several weeks, and the process is usually shared between women and their families. In wetland environments unsuitable for farming, sago allowed people to settle, and it is also an important element in local myths and rituals.

ranking.name: Sweet potato (kaukau)
ranking.description: Sweet potatoes are baked in the ashes of a fire or steamed in a mumu pit, giving a sweet, fluffy texture; they are the daily staple of highlanders.
ranking.history: The sweet potato originated in the Americas and reached the New Guinea highlands around the 17th century via trade routes through Southeast Asia, bringing about the so-called 'sweet potato revolution': it can grow at high altitudes and on poorer land, greatly increasing the highland population and making it possible to raise large numbers of pigs. 'Kaukau' is the Tok Pisin name, and today the sweet potato is the daily staple of highlanders and is also used to feed pigs.

ranking.name: Taro
ranking.description: Whole taro is boiled, roasted or steamed in a mumu, sometimes cooked together with coconut milk, with a creamy texture and a faint sweetness; it is the staple of coastal and island regions.
ranking.history: The use and cultivation of taro in New Guinea can be traced back seven to ten thousand years, and archaeologists have found evidence of taro and banana cultivation at the early agricultural site of Kuk in the highlands, making New Guinea one of the earliest regions in the world where agriculture developed independently. In many coastal and island societies, taro holds an important place in exchange ceremonies and festivals.

ranking.name: Aibika greens
ranking.description: The tender leaves of aibika are cooked with coconut milk and onions, sometimes with fish or meat, giving a smooth, slightly sticky texture similar to spinach.
ranking.history: Aibika (Abelmoschus manihot, of the okra genus) is the most important leafy green vegetable in Papua New Guinea, commonly grown in household gardens everywhere and rich in vitamins and protein. Because it is easily propagated from cuttings and can be harvested all year round, it has long been an important vegetable in the local diet, often eaten with staples such as taro and sweet potato, and is seen everywhere in markets.
